lead: A pump, turbine or pipe rarely holds a fixed mass. Fluid crosses its boundary all the time. For an open system at steady state, mass in equals mass out, and energy in equals energy out plus shaft work. The bookkeeping must include the work that pushes each stream across the boundary. That push work turns internal energy into enthalpy. The result is the steady-flow energy equation, used for steam turbines, compressors, nozzles and any control volume in a process plant.
prereq: You need: 1.3 for work and heat crossing a boundary, and 1.5 for ΔU = Q − W in a closed system.

blocks.text: A control volume is a chosen region of space. Its boundary may be a real casing or an imaginary surface in a pipe. Fluid crosses the boundary, so the control volume is an open system. At steady flow, properties at each fixed point inside and on the boundary do not change with time. The mass inside stays constant even though fluid keeps moving through. Mass entering must equal mass leaving. For several streams the balance is Σṁ_in = Σṁ_out. Here ṁ is mass flow rate in kg/s; in means entering the control volume, out means leaving. For one inlet 1 and one outlet 2, ṁ1 = ṁ2 = ṁ. Steady flow is not the same as no flow: a turbine at constant load is steady, while its start-up is not. The steady-flow energy equation applies only after this steady state is reached. This mass balance is the first equation for every open system.

blocks.where: ṁ is mass flow rate in kg/s; in and out mark streams entering and leaving the control volume.

blocks.text: A stream entering carries energy in three forms: internal energy u, kinetic energy V²/2 and potential energy gz, all per unit mass. It also carries flow work. To push fluid into the control volume, the upstream fluid does work Pv per unit mass; at the outlet the control volume pushes fluid out. The two push works combine with u into enthalpy. Define h = u + Pv. Here h is specific enthalpy in kJ/kg; u is specific internal energy in kJ/kg; P is pressure in kPa; v is specific volume in m³/kg, so Pv has units kJ/kg. Pv is called flow work, not shaft work. With Q positive into the system and W_s positive by the system, the steady-flow energy equation for any number of streams is Q − W_s = Σṁ_out(h + V²/2 + gz) − Σṁ_in(h + V²/2 + gz). Q is heat rate into the control volume in kW; W_s is shaft power by the control volume in kW; V is velocity in m/s; g = 9.81 m/s²; z is elevation in m. Each bracket is energy per kg, so multiply by ṁ in kg/s to get kW. Use consistent units: 1 kJ/kg = 1000 m²/s². Some syllabi call this the control-volume energy balance.

blocks.where: h is specific enthalpy in kJ/kg; u is specific internal energy in kJ/kg; P is pressure in kPa; v is specific volume in m³/kg; Pv is flow work in kJ/kg.

blocks.text: Q − W_s = Σṁ_out(h + V²/2 + gz) − Σṁ_in(h + V²/2 + gz)
blocks.where: Q is heat rate into the control volume in kW; W_s is shaft power by the control volume in kW; h is specific enthalpy in kJ/kg; V is velocity in m/s; g = 9.81 m/s²; z is elevation in m; ṁ is mass flow rate in kg/s.

blocks.text: For one inlet and one outlet with the same ṁ, divide by ṁ. The per-unit-mass form is q − w_s = (h2 − h1) + (V2² − V1²)/2 + g(z2 − z1). Here q = Q/ṁ is heat per unit mass in kJ/kg; w_s = W_s/ṁ is shaft work per unit mass in kJ/kg; subscript 1 is inlet and 2 is outlet. The equation says heat in minus shaft work out equals the rise in enthalpy plus kinetic plus potential energy. Many exam problems neglect Δpe or Δke. Neglect only after you estimate the term. A velocity change from 60 to 120 m/s gives Δke = 5.4 kJ/kg, small beside a steam enthalpy change of hundreds of kJ/kg. In a nozzle, however, Δke is the main output, so it cannot be dropped. In a turbine, h falls and W_s leaves; in a compressor, W_s enters and h rises. Sign errors are common: heat loss makes Q negative. The first law does not say Q = W_s; it says Q − W_s equals the net energy carried by the flow. Nozzles and compressors are worked out in 1.8.

blocks.where: q = Q/ṁ is heat per unit mass in kJ/kg; w_s = W_s/ṁ is shaft work per unit mass in kJ/kg; h is specific enthalpy in kJ/kg; V is velocity in m/s; z is elevation in m; subscript 1 is inlet and 2 is outlet.

figure.caption: Steam enters at 2.0 kg/s and 3200 kJ/kg, leaves at 2600 kJ/kg, and loses 50 kW of heat. The shaft power is the unknown.

spec.title: Steady-flow control volume
spec.aria: A block diagram shows a control volume with inlet steam at 2.0 kg/s and 3200 kJ/kg, outlet at 2600 kJ/kg, heat loss of 50 kW, and unknown shaft power.

examples.question: Steam enters a turbine at h1 = 3200 kJ/kg and V1 = 60 m/s. It leaves at h2 = 2600 kJ/kg and V2 = 120 m/s. The mass flow rate is 2.0 kg/s. Heat loss from the casing is 50 kW. Neglect potential energy. Find the shaft power.
steps: Use the steady-flow energy equation for one inlet and one outlet: Q − W_s = ṁ[(h2 − h1) + (V2² − V1²)/2].
Convert kinetic energy to kJ/kg: (V2² − V1²)/2 = (120² − 60²)/2 = 5400 J/kg = 5.4 kJ/kg.
Find the enthalpy change: h2 − h1 = 2600 − 3200 = −600 kJ/kg.
Add the specific energy change: −600 + 5.4 = −594.6 kJ/kg.
Heat loss is negative heat input: Q = −50 kW. Then −50 − W_s = −1189.2, so W_s = 1139.2 kW.
examples.answer: The turbine delivers a shaft power of 1139.2 kW, about 1.14 MW.
examples.check:
m_dot = 2.0
h1 = 3200.0
h2 = 2600.0
V1 = 60.0
V2 = 120.0
Q = -50.0
delta_h = h2 - h1
delta_ke = (V2**2 - V1**2) / (2 * 1000)
rhs = m_dot * (delta_h + delta_ke)
W_s = Q - rhs
print(W_s)

traps: Using u instead of h for a flowing stream: the flow work Pv is already in h. For a turbine or compressor, h is the property you look up in steam tables.
Dropping kinetic energy because it looks small: convert m²/s² to kJ/kg by dividing by 1000, then compare with Δh. 100 m/s gives 5 kJ/kg, not 5000 kJ/kg.
Sign slip on Q and W_s: Q is positive into the control volume; W_s is positive out. A 50 kW heat loss is Q = −50 kW, not +50 kW.
Treating flow work as shaft work: Pv is not W_s. W_s crosses the boundary through a shaft; Pv crosses with the fluid.
Applying the steady-flow equation during start-up or shutdown: at steady state the control volume stores no mass or energy; otherwise add a dE_cv/dt term.

quiz.q: Write the steady-flow mass balance for several inlets and outlets.
quiz.a: Σṁ_in = Σṁ_out, where ṁ is mass flow rate in kg/s.

quiz.q: Why does enthalpy appear instead of internal energy in the steady-flow energy equation?
quiz.a: A flowing stream carries flow work Pv as well as internal energy u. The sum u + Pv is h, so h groups both terms.

quiz.q: For one stream, q = 20 kJ/kg, w_s = 0, Δke = 0 and Δpe = 0. Find Δh.
quiz.a: q − w_s = Δh, so Δh = 20 kJ/kg.

quiz.q: Steam has h1 = 3000 kJ/kg and h2 = 2700 kJ/kg. Kinetic and potential changes are negligible and Q = 0. The mass flow is 1.5 kg/s. Find W_s.
A student uses u instead of h for a turbine. At inlet P1v1 = 1000 kJ/kg; at outlet P2v2 = 200 kJ/kg. What error results?
quiz.a: Using u omits the change in flow work. h1 − h2 exceeds u1 − u2 by P1v1 − P2v2 = 800 kJ/kg. The calculated work is too low by 800 kJ/kg for each kg flowing.

quiz.q: Why is Q = W_s wrong for a turbine even when Δke and Δpe are neglected?
quiz.a: The flow carries enthalpy in and out. The balance is Q − W_s = ṁ(h2 − h1). The enthalpy drop, not Q alone, supplies the shaft work.

quiz.q: Define control volume and steady flow.
quiz.a: A control volume is a chosen region with fluid crossing its boundary. Steady flow means properties at each fixed point do not change with time.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real plant energy balances add a storage term during start-up, shutdown and load changes. Exergy analysis extends the same control-volume idea to locate lost work. Pinch analysis uses stream enthalpies to design heat-exchanger networks. Computational fluid dynamics solves mass, momentum and energy balances at every small control volume.
